questions.question: Describe sea transport, the types of ships used and its advantages and disadvantages.
questions.expected_answer: Sea transport carries most international trade by volume. Container ships carry manufactured goods in standard containers, the largest more than twenty thousand TEUs; bulk carriers carry iron ore from Saldanha Bay, coal from Richards Bay, grain and manganese; tankers carry crude oil, fuel, chemicals and liquefied gas; reefers and refrigerated containers carry fruit, meat and fish such as South African citrus and grapes; ro-ro ships carry vehicles from Durban, Gqeberha and East London; and ferries and cruise ships carry passengers. It is the cheapest way to move large heavy loads over long distances and can cross oceans. However, it is slow, taking weeks to Europe or China, needs costly deep-water ports with cranes, storage and links, needs other modes at each end, can be delayed by storms, congestion and blocked routes, and pollutes through emissions, spills and waste. It suits heavy, bulky, low-value non-urgent goods and large container volumes; inland waterways such as the Rhine, Mississippi and Congo are also used.

questions.question: Compare air and road transport, giving advantages, disadvantages and uses.
questions.expected_answer: Air transport is the fastest over long distances and suits perishable goods such as cut flowers, fresh fish and berries, light valuable goods such as diamonds, gold, electronics and medicines, and urgent goods such as spare parts, vaccines and aid, and can reach remote areas; Kenya flies flowers to Europe and South Africa exports high-value goods from O. R. Tambo. But it is the most expensive per tonne, carries small loads, has high fuel use and emissions, needs costly airports and road links, and suffers weather delays. Road transport is the most flexible, delivering door-to-door without changing mode, with adjustable routes and schedules, suiting short and medium distances, smaller loads and areas without railways; most South African freight moves by road, and the N3 between Durban and Gauteng is one of Africa's busiest freight routes. But road is more expensive than rail and sea over long distances, carries smaller loads, damages roads, causes congestion, pollution and emissions, and has many fatal accidents.

questions.question: Describe rail and pipeline transport in South Africa and explain how a suitable mode is chosen.
questions.expected_answer: Rail efficiently carries heavy bulk goods over long distances, with one train replacing many trucks, lower cost, fuel and emissions per tonne, fixed schedules and greater safety for dangerous goods; examples are the Sishen to Saldanha iron ore line of about 860 km, the Mpumalanga to Richards Bay coal line, Metrorail and the Gautrain opened in 2010. But railways are expensive to build and maintain, need gentle gradients, require trucks at each end, are inflexible, and become unreliable when poorly maintained or when cables are stolen. Pipelines cheaply and continuously move liquids and gases once built, need few workers, are unaffected by traffic and weather and reduce tanker traffic; examples are the multi-product fuel pipeline of more than 500 km from Durban to Gauteng, gas pipelines from Mozambique and the Lesotho Highlands Water Project tunnels to the Vaal system. They are costly to build, carry only liquids and gases on fixed routes and risk leaks, fires and illegal tapping. A mode is chosen by the type of goods, distance, urgency, cost and available infrastructure, often combining modes intermodally, and considering emissions, which are lowest for sea and rail and highest for air.
